interactions.summary: Jiang and the room unpack wrath as mutual tearing-apart and self-destruction: anger bites others, drowns the angry person in the same force, and eventually consumes the body.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang prompt with student explanations and Jiang summary

interactions.summary: A student asks why the Styx appears here, and Jiang answers by treating it as a geographic threshold marking the descent from ordinary bad sins into sins that damage the fabric of the universe.
The packet ends with the start of Canto 8: the signal fires and Phlegyas's boat approaching across the marsh.

speaker_notes.note: The student's health example is colloquial and somewhat overstated, but the intended point is that anger rebounds on the self rather than only injuring others.

claims.claim: The room interprets the wrathful punishment as a scene where angry people tear others apart while simultaneously drowning in their own anger.
Jiang explicitly says anger makes you think you are hurting others when in fact you are also consuming yourself.
Jiang treats the Styx as a demarcation line in hell's geography, signaling entry into worse sins than lust, gluttony, greed, and anger as first encountered above.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive claim made in the seminar on 2026-06-21.

claims.claim: Below the Styx, Jiang says the sinners are no longer merely making life miserable but disrupting the fundamental structure of the universe.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive claim made in the seminar on 2026-06-21.

claims.claim: The reading at the end of the packet marks the concrete narrative transition into the next infernal threshold via tower signals and Phlegyas's boat.

signature_moments.moment: Wrath is redefined as an attempt to consume others that ends by consuming the self as well.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you're consuming others but you're also consuming yourself in the process
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's clearest compact diagnosis of anger in this section.

signature_moments.moment: Crossing the Styx stops being scenery and becomes a descent into sins that threaten the universe's structure.
signature_moments.source_phrase: destroying the very fabric of the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This raises the stakes of Dante's geography from moral taxonomy to cosmological order.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's phrase for the geographic thresholds in inferno, purgatory, and paradise that mark entry into a new moral level.

chronology_notes.note: This June 21, 2026 packet turns from reflective punishment within a single sin to a larger map of infernal descent, with the Styx functioning as the threshold into more universe-distorting forms of evil.

uncertainty_notes.note: The first student response on wrath is partially garbled, but the line of thought about biting or tearing others in anger is recoverable.
